```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7,
                      fig.height = 3.5)
library(modelterms7)
set.seed(1)
```

In many fitting functions a term in a model formula is a string on which the
function switches. Writing a new term then means editing that function, and a
user cannot write one at all. Here a term is an object. It builds its own
design block, carries its own penalty, reports its number of parameters and
reapplies itself to new data. A formula interpreter recognizes a term by the
value that its call *returns*, so a term defined outside the package works in
a formula with no edit anywhere.

This vignette writes a term that the package does not ship: a seasonal term,
a Fourier design of $2k$ columns over a known period, penalized so that the
higher harmonics shrink first.

## The minimal additive term

A new additive term is a subclass of `additive_term` together with a method
for `term_build()`. State that belongs to the term is declared as
properties of its own subclass; the shipped `SmoothTerm` carries `vars`,
`by`, `spec` and `sparse` in this way.

```{r}
SeasonTerm <- S7::new_class(
  "SeasonTerm", parent = additive_term,
  properties = list(expr = S7::class_any, spec = S7::class_list)
)
```

The constructor captures the covariate unevaluated and records the
settings that the build needs. The constructor computes nothing, because a
specification is not a block and the data are not yet in scope.

```{r}
season <- function(x, period, k = 3, lambda = NULL) {
  xe <- substitute(x)
  SeasonTerm(
    label = sprintf("season(%s)", deparse(xe)),
    expr = xe,
    spec = list(period = period, k = k),
    hyper = if (is.null(lambda)) list() else list(lambda = lambda),
    X = NULL, coef_names = character(0),
    blueprint = list(), penalty = NULL
  )
}
```

`term_build()` evaluates the expression in the data and fills `X`,
`coef_names`, `blueprint` and `penalty`. The blueprint stores what
`term_predict()` needs later, so that prediction reapplies recorded quantities
and does not recompute them from the new rows. Storing the blueprint at build
time is the second requirement on a new term.

```{r}
.season_X <- function(x, period, k) {
  j <- seq_len(k)
  w <- outer(2 * pi * x / period, j)
  X <- cbind(cos(w), sin(w))
  colnames(X) <- c(sprintf("cos%d", j), sprintf("sin%d", j))
  X
}

S7::method(term_build, SeasonTerm) <- function(term, data, ...) {
  x <- as.numeric(eval(term@expr, data, baseenv()))
  sp <- term@spec
  S7::set_props(
    term,
    X = .season_X(x, sp$period, sp$k),
    coef_names = c(sprintf("cos%d", seq_len(sp$k)),
                   sprintf("sin%d", seq_len(sp$k))),
    blueprint = sp,
    penalty = penalties7::quadratic_penalty(diag(rep(seq_len(sp$k)^2, 2)))
  )
}
```

The penalty is the quadratic form $\tfrac{\lambda}{2}\sum_j j^2(a_j^2 + b_j^2)$,
plus the normalizing constant of the corresponding Gaussian prior, where $a_j$
and $b_j$ are the cosine and sine coefficients of harmonic $j$ and $\lambda$ is
the smoothing parameter. Harmonic $j$ oscillates $j$ times as fast, so the
weight $j^2$ penalizes the higher harmonics more strongly, and $\lambda$
controls the smoothness of the fit as well as its size.

The constructor and the `term_build()` method are the whole of the compulsory
part. The term can now be built on data:

```{r}
d <- data.frame(t = seq(0, 4, length.out = 200))
d$y <- 2 * sin(2 * pi * d$t) + 0.4 * cos(6 * pi * d$t) + rnorm(200, sd = 0.3)

tm <- term_build(season(t, period = 1, k = 3), d)
c(built = term_is_built(tm), npar = term_npar(tm))
term_coef_names(tm)
dim(term_matrix(tm))
```

A least-squares fit on the block recovers the coefficients that generated the
data:

```{r}
cf <- lm.fit(cbind(1, term_matrix(tm)), d$y)$coefficients
names(cf) <- c("(Intercept)", term_coef_names(tm))
round(cf, 3)
```

The truth is `sin1 = 2`, `cos3 = 0.4` and zero for the other coefficients.

## Prediction at new data

`term_predict()` has no base method, so a term that is used for prediction or
for cross-validation defines one. The method reapplies the blueprint:

```{r}
S7::method(term_predict, SeasonTerm) <- function(term, newdata, ...) {
  x <- as.numeric(eval(term@expr, newdata, baseenv()))
  bp <- term@blueprint
  .season_X(x, bp$period, bp$k)
}
```

The period comes from the blueprint and never from the new data. A term that
recomputed it would be a different term on every subset. The identity that
detects this mistake is that prediction on the rows of the fit must return the
block of the fit:

```{r}
rows <- c(3, 40, 111)
all.equal(term_predict(tm, d[rows, , drop = FALSE]),
          term_matrix(tm)[rows, , drop = FALSE], check.attributes = FALSE)
```

For a seasonal term the period is a constant that the caller supplied, so the
hazard is small. For a spline the recorded quantities are the knots, and for a
factor they are the levels. Each is learned from the fitting data, and each
would silently change if it were learned again at prediction.

The `baseenv()` enclosure is deliberate. The expression is evaluated in the new
data with only the base namespace behind it, so a variable of the calling
environment is not found. Under any other enclosure such a variable would be
picked up from the calling environment and would quietly supply the fitting
data's values.

## Validating the term

`check_term()` builds the term and runs six checks on the result:

```{r}
print(check_term(season(t, period = 1, k = 3), d, verbose = FALSE))
```

The last check builds the term on all the rows, calls `term_predict()` on a
subset of them and compares the result with the corresponding rows of the
block. A term that rebuilds its basis or relearns its levels at prediction
fails this check. When the data carry a factor, the subset omits every row of
the factor's last level; otherwise it is the first half of the rows, as here.
The subset is passed through `droplevels()` first, because a plain row subset
of a data frame keeps every factor level, including levels that do not occur
in any row, and a term that rebuilt its levels would look correct on it.

## The penalty and its rank

The penalty travels with the term, so the effective degrees of freedom follow
from the term alone:

```{r}
H <- crossprod(term_matrix(tm))
c(`lambda = 1` = edf(tm, cf[-1], H, theta = list(lambda = 1)),
  `lambda = 1e6` = edf(tm, cf[-1], H, theta = list(lambda = 1e6)))
```

The count runs from 6 down to 0, because the penalty above has full rank:
every coefficient is penalized, so a large smoothing parameter removes the
seasonal effect entirely. A shipped `s()` with its default smoother has a
penalty that is rank deficient by exactly one, so that the effective count runs
from the number of coefficients down to one, and the limit is a straight
line. The cyclic, Fourier and first-order smoothers have no free line, and
their count goes to zero. Which of the two behaviors a term has depends on the
null space of its penalty, and the choice of that null space is a modeling
decision.

`term_penalties()` reports the entries that a term declares. Each entry names a
subset of the term's own parameters and the penalty over them, together with
the hyperparameters that are held and the settings of the path over the others.
One entry that covers every parameter is the ordinary case:

```{r}
length(term_penalties(tm))
names(term_penalties(tm)[[1]])
```

A term with several penalties declares several entries. A `jseg()` whose
developments carry a penalty on each kind of coefficient is an example: one
entry covers the changes of slope and another the changes of level. A slope
change and a jump are not comparable quantities, and one hyperparameter over
their union would price them against each other. A `jseg()` written without
developments declares no entry.

```{r}
jj <- term_build(jseg(t, gamma ~ 0 + lasso(~ 1), delta ~ 0 + ridge(~ 1)), d)
vapply(term_penalties(jj), function(e) e$name, character(1))
length(term_penalties(term_build(jseg(t), d)))
```

## In a formula

`interpret_formula()` recognizes a term by evaluating its call and testing
whether the value inherits `model_term`. The term names are never listed, so
the new term is recognized with no edit:

```{r}
d$x <- rnorm(nrow(d))
f <- interpret_formula(y ~ x + season(t, period = 1), data = d)
vapply(f$terms, function(z) class(z)[[1]], character(1))
```

A bare covariate collapses into one parametric block. A call whose value does
not inherit `model_term` stays a covariate when a model matrix can hold the
value, so `log(x)` is arithmetic. A call whose evaluation fails signals an
error that names the call.

Recognition by evaluation also produces a third case, a masked name. `mgcv`
exports `s()` and `te()`, and `segmented` exports `seg()`, so a user who has
attached either package and writes this package's formula gets the function
of the other package. The interpreter rejects the result at the call itself.
The error names the term, the class of the value and the package that
supplied the function, and it suggests `modelterms7::`, so the value does not
reach `model.matrix()` and fail there.

## Inherited methods and structural terms

`term_matrix()`, `term_coef_names()`, `term_npar()`, `term_penalty()`,
`term_value()`, `term_smooth()`, `edf()`, `print()` and `plot()` are inherited
from the base classes and read the properties that `term_build()` filled.

Two further generics matter only for a term whose block moves with its
coefficients. `term_refresh()` recomputes the block at new coefficients.
`term_jacobian_block()` reports whether that block is a Jacobian, so that the
fitting step is Gauss-Newton, or a frozen working linearization, so that the
step is a fixed-point iteration. For `nl()`, `seg()` and every smoothed
break-point term, the answer is `TRUE`. For a sharp `jump()` or `jseg()`, the
answer is `FALSE`, because its break-point is read off a product of
coefficients and is not estimated as a parameter. A term with a fixed design,
like the one above, inherits a `term_refresh()` that returns the term
unchanged and a `term_jacobian_block()` that returns `TRUE`, and it needs
neither method.

The other branch of the class tree is `structural_term`, whose terms rewrite
the likelihood instead of adding columns: `gas()` drives a distribution
parameter by a score-driven recursion, and `regime()` mixes the likelihood over
a latent Markov chain. A structural term has a different structure. It supplies
`term_params()`, `term_links()` and `term_npar()`, and either `term_filter()`
or `term_loglik()`, and `term_adjoint()` carries the derivative of a filter.
`statmodels7::statmod()` fits at most one structural term in a formula.

## Summary

* Minimum to define an additive term: a subclass of `additive_term` and a
  `term_build()` method that fills `X`, `coef_names`, `blueprint` and
  `penalty`. Any state of its own is a property of the subclass.
* The constructor captures the covariate unevaluated and computes nothing.
* `term_predict()` has no base method. Write one, reapply the blueprint, and
  evaluate in the new data with `baseenv()` as the enclosure.
* `check_term()` runs six checks, and the last one runs on a `droplevels()`
  subset, which exposes a rebuild.
* The null space of the penalty determines what a large smoothing parameter
  leaves behind, and `edf()` follows from the term alone.
* `interpret_formula()` recognizes a term by evaluating its call, so a term
  defined outside the package needs no registration.
* A block that moves with its coefficients adds `term_refresh()` and
  `term_jacobian_block()`; a term that rewrites the likelihood belongs to the
  other branch.
